title: Markets Outlook
intro:
Hotter US Inflation Triggers Tech Selloff as Investors Reassess Fed Policy
US Stocks Suffer Sharp Losses as Rate-Hike Risks Rise

Wall Street suffered its steepest selloff since late July on Wednesday as hotter-than-expected US inflation data revived concerns about further Federal Reserve tightening. Technology and AI-related stocks led the decline, while defensive healthcare shares attracted buying interest as investors reduced exposure to growth-oriented assets.

The S&P 500 fell 1.11% to 7,718.94, recording its fifth decline in six sessions since its October 6 record high. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.9% to 26,692.87, while the Russell 2000 lost 1.9% to 2,729.53. The Dow Jones Industrial Average proved more resilient, slipping just 0.1% to 51,621.48.
September headline CPI rose 3.7% year-over-year, above expectations of 3.6%, while core CPI increased 0.3% month-over-month against forecasts of 0.2%. Gasoline prices, up approximately 34% from a year earlier, contributed to persistent inflationary pressure.

The figures complicated the Fed's policy outlook, particularly as rising energy costs threaten to keep inflation elevated. Markets reassessed the likelihood of additional rate increases, although pricing remained volatile and policymakers continued to signal caution. Higher borrowing costs would pose a challenge for equities, particularly companies whose valuations depend on future earnings growth.

AI and Semiconductor Stocks Lead the Decline
The technology selloff intensified as investors questioned the sustainability of debt-financed AI infrastructure investment. CoreWeave plunged 15.5% after stress emerged in its bond market, with yields approaching 15%, raising concerns about financing costs and credit risk across the sector.
Oracle dropped 8.8% following developments involving a proposed energy-service agreement for its New Mexico AI data center. Nebius Group fell approximately 10%, while major chipmakers also suffered significant losses. Nvidia declined 3.2%, Broadcom lost 3.1%, and AMD tumbled 5.7%.
The pressure reflects a growing concern that higher interest rates could undermine the economics of the AI investment boom. Data centers require substantial upfront capital, reliable energy supplies and long-term financing. If borrowing costs remain elevated, investors may become increasingly selective about which companies can translate massive AI spending into sustainable profits.
The latest session therefore highlighted a potential vulnerability in the market's technology-led rally: strong long-term demand for AI does not eliminate the risks associated with valuations, financing and execution.

Banking Sector Faces Earnings and Regulatory Pressure
Bank of America fell nearly 5% after reporting weaker-than-expected profits and trading revenue, while also disclosing a regulatory fine of approximately $1.21 billion related to money-laundering and sanctions violations.
The results added another source of pressure to a market already dealing with higher inflation and uncertainty over monetary policy. Banks must balance lending profitability against funding costs, credit quality and regulatory risks. Persistently high rates may support some lending margins, but they can also increase pressure on borrowers and financial markets.

Healthcare Outperforms as Investors Seek Defensive Exposure
Healthcare was among the few bright spots, gaining more than 2% as investors rotated toward defensive sectors.
Bristol-Myers Squibb rose 4.6%, while UnitedHealth Group advanced approximately 4.7%.
Eight of the S&P 500's 11 sectors finished lower, underscoring the broad nature of the selloff. The relative strength in healthcare suggests investors are becoming more cautious about the economic and financial outlook, although one session is not sufficient to establish a lasting defensive rotation.
Elsewhere, Liquidia surged 26.6% after settling its litigation with United Therapeutics through a $380.7 million global agreement.
Bending Spoons jumped 41% following Berkshire Hathaway's additional $330 million investment.
In after-hours trading, Rocket Lab shares came under pressure after the company delayed the first launch of its Neutron rocket.
Netflix also announced plans to cut approximately 1,000 jobs.

UK Economy Returns to Growth
The UK economy expanded by 0.1% month-over-month in August, following growth of 0.4% in both June and July.
The result exceeded expectations for a 0.1% contraction, with stronger production offsetting weakness in services and construction.
Annual GDP growth reached 2.1%, the strongest increase since October 2022. Although the data offered some reassurance about economic resilience, the slowdown in monthly growth suggests the recovery remains uneven.
For sterling, the outlook will continue to depend on the balance between economic activity, inflation and expectations for Bank of England policy.
Stronger growth can provide support, but persistent inflation and restrictive monetary conditions remain important constraints.

European Markets Under Pressure
European equities were set for a weaker opening as the global technology selloff spread across markets.
Euro Stoxx 50 futures fell 0.9%, while Stoxx 600 futures declined 0.5%.
Investors were also assessing the implications of stronger US inflation for global borrowing costs.
The immediate focus turned to UK GDP, French inflation and eurozone industrial production.
Corporate earnings offered a mixed picture. Ericsson reported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings, supported by demand for mobile network equipment, while Pernod Ricard recorded a smaller-than-expected sales decline.
Nordea Bank, however, missed earnings expectations amid narrower lending margins.
The European outlook remains sensitive to global risk appetite, energy prices and the trajectory of interest rates.
A sustained deterioration in US technology shares could weigh on European indices, particularly sectors with significant exposure to global growth and industrial demand.

FX, Bonds and Commodities: Markets Reassess the Inflation Outlook
The US dollar index retreated toward 102 after recently reaching an 18-month high, as investors continued to evaluate the implications of September's inflation data.
The dollar weakened against the euro, sterling and New Zealand dollar, suggesting that the immediate reaction to inflation was more nuanced than a straightforward shift toward a stronger US currency.
Government bonds attracted safe-haven demand during the equity selloff. Japan's 10-year government bond yield fell approximately seven basis points to 2.93%, reaching a five-week low. This decline reflected the broader movement toward defensive assets, despite ongoing expectations that the Bank of Japan could continue normalizing monetary policy.

Gold recovered toward $4,150 per ounce, supported by a softer dollar and lower bond yields. However, expectations of tighter Fed policy remain a potential headwind because higher real yields generally increase the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets.
Oil prices also retreated as Brent crude fell toward $104 per barrel following its recent rally. Profit-taking and technical correction appeared to contribute to the decline, while investors assessed reports concerning a possible easing of US sanctions.
The pullback in crude could offer some relief on the inflation front, although energy prices remain a significant source of uncertainty.

Intermarket Analysis: Inflation Remains the Key Driver
The latest market reaction highlights the importance of the relationship between inflation, interest rates, equities and commodities.
Higher inflation can push market yields upward by reducing expectations for monetary easing and increasing the perceived risk of further tightening.
This is particularly challenging for technology stocks, whose valuations are often more sensitive to changes in discount rates. At the same time, a broad equity selloff can trigger safe-haven demand for government bonds, causing yields to fall even as inflation remains elevated.
This explains why the current cross-asset picture is not entirely consistent: inflation concerns remain strong, but defensive flows are supporting bonds and gold, while the dollar has weakened from recent highs.
Oil remains another critical variable. A sustained decline in crude prices could help ease inflation expectations and reduce pressure on central banks.
Conversely, renewed energy-price gains could complicate the policy outlook and increase volatility across currencies, bonds and equities.

Market Outlook: Volatility Likely to Remain Elevated
Markets are entering a more delicate phase as investors reassess the outlook for monetary policy and the sustainability of the AI-driven rally. The latest CPI report has challenged expectations for an easier policy environment, while the selloff in AI infrastructure stocks has exposed concerns about leverage and financing costs.

For US equities, the Nasdaq and Russell 2000 appear particularly vulnerable to further repricing if yields rise again. The S&P 500's ability to stabilize following its latest decline will be important in determining whether this is a short-term correction or the beginning of a deeper pullback.

In FX markets, the dollar's next move will depend on whether inflation concerns translate into firmer rate expectations or whether weaker risk appetite and safe-haven flows dominate. Gold may benefit from lower yields and dollar weakness, but a renewed rise in real yields could limit its recovery.
The key variables to monitor are upcoming Fed commentary, Treasury yields, oil prices and the next round of corporate earnings.

Overall Bias: Cautious on equities, particularly high-valuation technology and AI-related stocks, while favoring a selective approach to defensive sectors. The broader outlook remains highly dependent on the interaction between inflation, energy prices and interest-rate expectations. A sustained stabilization in yields and oil would improve the environment for risk assets; renewed increases in either would raise the risk of further market weakness.
